Curative-intent ifosfamide, cisplatin, and etoposide (ICE) was started because of the prolonged remission, biopsy-proven recurrence, and anticipated chemosensitivity. The planned 28-day regimen comprised ifosfamide 900 mg/m2, cisplatin 20 mg/m2, and etoposide 100 mg/m2 on days 1–5. Scheduled oral desmopressin 360 μg/day, hydrocortisone 30 mg/day, and levothyroxine 50 μg/day were continued during the sodium disturbances following endocrinology consultation, which supported maintenance of the established doses and schedules. Before salvage chemotherapy, serum sodium was 139.3 mEq/L, measured serum osmolality was 278 mOsm/kg, serum creatinine was 0.52 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate was 163.4 mL/min/1.73 m2, spot urinary sodium was 91.4 mEq/L, and urine osmolality was 555 mOsm/kg. Baseline cortisol was reported as 5.5 μg/dL, but sampling time relative to hydrocortisone was unavailable, and the value was not used to infer adrenal reserve. Baseline laboratory results are provided in Online Resource 3. The course of serum sodium and serum osmolality, oral sodium supplementation, treatment modifications, and urinary sodium/osmolality trends during ICE are shown in Fig. 3a, b. After ICE cycle 1, fatigue, anorexia, and headache accompanied grade 4 hypotonic hyponatremia (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events [CTCAE] version 5.0): serum sodium reached 118.4 mEq/L on cycle 1 day 9, and measured serum osmolality was 236 mOsm/kg. The hyponatremia was managed with fluid restriction to 1.0 L/day and intravenous 3% hypertonic saline administered at 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours, which raised serum sodium to 124.1 mEq/L over 24 hours. The rate of correction was monitored every 4 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination, and hypertonic saline was discontinued once serum sodium exceeded 125 mEq/L. Oral sodium chloride tablets (1 g every 8 hours) were added as a bridge to maintain serum sodium above 130 mEq/L. Desmopressin was temporarily held for 48 hours, after which it was resumed at a reduced dose of 180 μg/day in consultation with endocrinology, given the concern that the prior dose may have contributed to the degree of water retention. Cisplatin, a well-recognized cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and, paradoxically, of SIADH-like presentations, was considered a potential contributor to the electrolyte derangement, although the temporal relationship and the pre-existing SIADH phenotype made a multifactorial etiology most likely. ICE cycle 2 was delayed by 14 days to allow full recovery of serum sodium to 138.6 mEq/L and to stabilize the endocrine regimen.
